title: Ordway Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Ordway wells have a median depth of 18 feet; finished well costs are modeled at $6,600-$13,000.
h1: Ordway, Colorado Well Depths, Water and Drilling Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Ordway means dealing with unusually shallow recorded wells, but not necessarily simple water decisions. Colorado DWR permit records within 5 miles show 133 wells, with 86 reporting a total depth and 74 recorded as constructed. The records do not include pump-yield results or static water levels, so a nearby permit is useful for understanding construction patterns, not proof that a new well will produce a specific amount.

Ordway sits on plains terrain where the records identify mostly unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with only a small number listed as alluvial. Sugar City, Crowley and Manzanola provide useful nearby comparison points, but the lot itself still controls the drilling result.

sections.heading: Ordway wells are usually very shallow
sections.html:
The recorded median well depth near Ordway is 18 feet. The middle half runs from 15 to 40 feet, and 98% of the depth records are under 100 feet. For a driller, that pattern suggests many bids may involve a short hole through alluvium or plains sediment rather than a deep production well.

There are exceptions. The 90th-percentile depth is 68 feet, and the deepest record reaches 1,736 feet. One unusually deep permit should not set your budget, but it does show that local geology is not uniform. Ask for a site-specific estimate and confirm casing, grout, access and completion assumptions before comparing bids.

sections.heading: The records do not tell you the well yield
sections.html:
None of the 133 permitted wells reports a pump yield in the available records. That is the most important limitation for a buyer: the 18-foot median describes depth, not how much water a well can deliver. A shallow well may be adequate for an existing household, while another lot may need testing, rehabilitation or a different completion plan.

Use neighboring permits as clues, especially around Sugar City, Crowley and Rocky Ford, but do not treat them as a guaranteed water supply. Have a driller evaluate the proposed point, ask how the well will be tested, and make sure the intended household, stock or irrigation use matches the permit conditions.

sections.heading: No local water-level series is available
sections.html:
The Ordway-area records contain no reported static water levels. Because there is no water-level-by-decade series here, the data cannot establish that the water table is dropping, stable or rising. A shallow median depth may reflect local conditions in the completed wells, but it does not replace a measurement on the property you are considering.

Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, covering 130 wells, while 3 name an alluvial aquifer. That naming pattern reinforces the need for a site-specific evaluation. Before closing, ask for any existing well tests, production history and maintenance records, then verify the permit and allowed use with Colorado DWR.

sections.heading: Ordway drilling records are concentrated in the 2000s
sections.html:
Permit history is heavily weighted toward the 2000s, when 66 permits were issued. The records also show 16 permits from the 1970s, 9 from the 1990s, 5 from the 1950s, 3 from the 1980s and 2 from the 1960s. The newest permit year is 2020.

Authorized (Pe, Pg) is the most active driller in these records, with 53 wells. Hoffman (Hoffman, Earl) appears on 7, and Eastwood Drilling (Eastwood, Francis) on 3. Those names describe recorded permit history, not a recommendation or proof that any driller is available now. Confirm licensing, insurance, references and the proposed completion method.

sections.heading: A shallow Ordway well can still have a full project cost
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $35-$55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 18-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $600-$1,000. That is only the hole, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $6,600-$13,000. Get a written bid that separates drilling from casing, grout, pump equipment, pressure tank, power, trenching, water testing and permits. The deepest recorded well is 1,736 feet, so a lot with different geology could fall far outside the median-depth example.

sections.heading: Check water quality, yield and the building plan
sections.html:
Environmental review matters around Ordway. Within about 10 miles, the mapped records show 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not prove a private well is contaminated, but it is a reason to test existing or new water and learn the local site history before relying on it.

There are also no reported yields, so low production and an unsuccessful hole remain risks that a permit count cannot remove. Confirm the well location, septic layout, setbacks, access for a rig and the electrical route before building. A household well permit is not automatically authorization for irrigation or other uses; check the DWR permit and any augmentation requirements that apply.

sections.heading: Buy the lot only after verifying its water plan
sections.html:
For an existing home, inspect the well equipment, pressure behavior, storage, treatment and recent water test rather than relying on the 18-foot area median. Request the permit number, construction record and service history. For vacant land, have a Colorado-licensed driller review the proposed location and give a written drilling and completion estimate before your inspection deadline.

Compare nearby records in Ordway with properties toward Sugar City, Crowley and Manzanola, but keep the comparison practical: the available data gives depth patterns and permit history, not a dependable yield or water-level forecast. Price the complete system, plan septic and access together, and make the purchase contract protect you if the well is dry, weak or unsuitable for the intended use.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Ordway, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth within 5 miles of Ordway is 18 feet. The middle half of reported depths falls from 15 to 40 feet, and 98% are under 100 feet. There are exceptions, including a deepest recorded well of 1,736 feet, so a nearby shallow permit does not guarantee the same result on your lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Ordway?
faq.a: The local model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 18-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $600-$1,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $6,600-$13,000. Actual pricing depends on geology, access, casing, completion requirements and the equipment your property needs.

faq.q: Do Ordway wells produce enough water for a house?
faq.a: The available records cannot answer that directly because 0 wells report a pump yield. Depth is not the same as production. Before buying, request any existing production history, have a driller evaluate the site, and confirm that the permit allows the intended household use. A nearby well is evidence, not a guarantee.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Ordway, Colorado?
faq.a: Testing is necessary. The mapped area has 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those locations do not prove contamination at a particular well, but they justify testing existing or new water and reviewing local environmental history before drinking it.

faq.q: Who has drilled wells near Ordway, Colorado?
faq.a: The permit records list Authorized (Pe, Pg) on 53 wells, Hoffman (Hoffman, Earl) on 7, and Eastwood Drilling (Eastwood, Francis) on 3. These are historical permit records, not endorsements or confirmation of current availability. Verify licensing, insurance, references, scope of work and the proposed completion method before hiring.
